chapters.title: The square is not a detail
chapters.dek: A variance swap and a volatility swap on the same underlying, over the same window, do not have the same fair value. The gap is Jensen's inequality, and it is large.

figures.title: Realized volatility as a distribution, and the two fair strikes
figures.caption: Notice the two markers separating as you raise vol of vol, and notice that only one of them moves. The mean of the distribution stays pinned at the center while the variance strike walks to the right, because the right tail is being squared and the left tail cannot go below zero. That one-sidedness is why the product is quoted the way it is.

checks.q: A dealer quotes you a variance swap at 25 and a volatility swap on the same window at 25. Which is cheaper for you to buy?
checks.right: The variance swap, because its fair strike is above the volatility swap's — quoting them equal means the variance swap is being sold below fair value
checks.why: The variance swap. Its fair strike carries the convexity premium — 2.08 points at a vol of vol of 0.4 — so a variance swap quoted at the volatility swap's level is being handed to you cheap. The last answer is the tempting one, because it sounds appropriately humble, but the comparison is between two fair values today and does not require knowing the outcome.

terms.Vol of vol: How much the realized volatility itself varies. It is the second-order uncertainty: not how much the stock moves, but how uncertain you are about how much it will move.

chapters.text: People say "volatility" and write down variance, and most of the time nothing goes wrong. It goes wrong here. Variance is the square of volatility, squaring is a convex function, and the expectation of a convex function is not the function of the expectation. So the fair strike of a contract paying realized variance sits strictly above the square of the fair strike of one paying realized volatility — on the same underlying, over the same window, with nothing else different. The size of the gap is set by how uncertain the volatility itself is. If you knew realized vol would be exactly 25%, the two contracts would be identical and the gap would be zero. Put some uncertainty around that 25% and the gap opens immediately. The figure draws realized volatility as a distribution centered on 25 and reports both numbers. At a vol-of-vol of 0.4 the mean volatility is still 25.0% but the square root of mean variance is 27.1% — a gap of 2.08 volatility points . Push vol-of-vol to 0.6 and the gap is 4.93 points , which is not a rounding difference, it is most of a trade. This matters in one direction more than the other. Someone short a variance swap is short that convexity: their losses grow with the square of how wrong they were, while their gains are capped by volatility not being able to fall below zero. That asymmetry is the whole risk profile of the product and chapter 05 returns to it. [equation: E[σ_R²] > (E[σ_R])² whenever σ_R is uncertain] Reads as: the average of the squares beats the square of the average. The two are equal only when there is nothing to average over — that is, when you already know the answer. chapters.title: One contract whose hedge pays exactly the variance
chapters.dek: Not approximately, and not on average. On every path, to five decimals.

figures.title: Hedged P&L against realized variance, one dot per path
figures.caption: The lower panel is the explanation for the upper one. The call's dollar gamma is a hill — it measures movement only where it is standing. The log contract's is a flat line, so it measures movement everywhere equally, and "everywhere equally" is the definition of variance. Raise the hedge count and the dots tighten onto the diagonal; drop it to twelve and they scatter, because you are now sampling the variance rather than measuring it.

checks.q: Why can't you build a variance meter out of a single at-the-money straddle, delta-hedged?
checks.right: Its dollar gamma is a hill centered on the strike, so it measures movement near the strike and ignores movement far from it. The measurement depends on where the stock goes, not just how much it moves
checks.why: The dollar gamma is not flat. A hedged straddle is a perfectly good approximation to a variance position while spot stays near the strike, which is why it is used that way in practice, and it decays into something else entirely once the stock trends away. The whole point of the 1/K² strip in chapter 03 is to add up enough hills to make a flat surface.

terms.Dollar gamma: S²Γ. The gamma exposure measured in money rather than in shares-per-dollar. It is what decides how much a delta hedge earns from a move of a given percentage size.

chapters.text: Page 01 delta-hedged a call and found a residual that shrank with effort but never vanished. Here is a payoff that behaves completely differently. Take the log contract — a claim paying −(2/T)·ln(S_T/S_0) at expiry — delta-hedge it mechanically, and add up the money at the end. The answer is the realized variance of the path. Every time. The figure runs a few thousand paths and plots each one's hedged P&L against the realized variance it actually delivered. The result is not a cloud with a trend through it, it is a line : hedging daily, the correlation between the two is 0.99998 at 10 volatility and still 0.99966 at 45. Mean hedged P&L matches mean realized variance to five decimal places. The figure opens at thirty volatility and sixty-three hedges rather than 252, where the same correlation reads 0.99946 — the gap is discretization, and dragging the hedge count to the top closes it. The reason is a single structural fact. A delta-hedged option's P&L over a small step is ½·S²Γ·(realized − implied) — the gamma rent from page 01. That expression is weighted by dollar gamma , which for a normal option is a bump centered on the strike — so an ordinary option pays you for movement near its strike and almost nothing for movement far away. The log contract's dollar gamma is constant . It pays the same for a 1% move wherever the stock happens to be, which is precisely what "measure the variance" means. So the log contract is not one instrument among many. It is the unique payoff that turns a delta hedge into a variance meter, and everything in the rest of this page is an attempt to build it out of things that actually trade. [equation: hedged P&L = σ_R² because S²Γ is constant] Reads as: a contract that pays the same for a percentage move at any price level accumulates exactly the sum of squared percentage moves. Constant dollar gamma is the whole trick. Hedged P&L against realized variance, one dot per path Dollar gamma: an ordinary call against the log contract The experiment The lower panel is the explanation for the upper one. The call's dollar gamma is a hill — it measures movement only where it is standing. The log contract's is a flat line, so it measures movement everywhere equally, and "everywhere equally" is the definition of variance. Raise the hedge count and the dots tighten onto the diagonal; drop it to twelve and they scatter, because you are now sampling the variance rather than measuring it. Try this Drop the number of hedges to 12 and predict whether the dots move off the line in a biased direction or just spread around it. Derivation — why constant dollar gamma means variance Hold a payoff f(S) and hedge its delta continuously. Itô says the value change splits into a delta piece, which the hedge cancels, and a curvature piece, which it does not. [equation: d(hedged) = ½ · f″(S) · S²σ² dt] Reads as: what survives the hedge is curvature multiplied by the size of the move squared. This is page 01's gamma rent with the implied leg removed. Now choose f(S) = −(2/T)·ln(S) . Differentiating twice gives f″(S) = (2/T)/S² , so the S² cancels exactly. [equation: ½ · (2/T)/S² · S²σ² dt = (σ²/T) dt] Reads as: the price level drops out and you are left accumulating variance per unit time. Integrate over the life and the total is the realized variance. That cancellation is the entire subject. It happens for the logarithm and for nothing else, which is why the log contract has a name. Where it breaks. Itô's lemma assumes the path is continuous. A jump moves the stock a finite distance with no intervening hedge, so the hedge does not cancel the delta piece and the log contract stops measuring quadratic variation — chapter 07 puts a number on it. Discrete hedging causes scatter but no bias, which is the difference the try-this box above is asking you to notice. And the derivation says nothing about how you would own f(S) , which is the next chapter's problem.

chapters.title: Building it out of things that trade
chapters.dek: Nobody lists a log contract. You assemble one from ordinary options weighted by 1/K², and then never touch it again.

figures.title: The strip's payoff converging onto the log contract
figures.caption: Watch the corners rather than the overall shape — the strip is already roughly right with six strikes, and what the extra strikes buy is the removal of kinks between them. Each kink is a place where your replication is a straight line and the true payoff is curved, which is exactly where a variance measurement goes missing.

checks.q: Why does the strip need no rebalancing when page 01's replication did?
checks.right: Because the option portfolio reproduces the payoff's curvature exactly and for all time — only the delta hedge moves, and that is the part doing the measuring
checks.why: The curvature is matched exactly, once. A payoff decomposed into options by its own second derivative is not an approximation that decays — the identity holds at every spot and every time, so the basket is bought and left. This is what "static replication" means and it is the genuinely new machinery on this page. The third answer describes something that would be very convenient and does not exist: the weights are fixed at inception.

chapters.text: The log payoff is a curve, and the only curves you can buy are made of options. Any twice-differentiable payoff can be written exactly as a fixed portfolio of calls and puts, with each strike weighted by the payoff's second derivative there. For the log contract that second derivative is (2/T)/K² — so the weight on the option struck at K is proportional to 1/K² , and that is where the famous weighting comes from. It is not a convention or an approximation. It is the curvature of a logarithm. What makes this different from every other hedge in the series is that it is static . You buy the strip once, at inception, and you do not rebalance it. Page 01's replication needed continuous attention and still left a residual; page 13 puts a price on that attention. Here the options portfolio is fixed at the start and the only ongoing work is the delta hedge, which is the part that does the measuring. The figure builds the strip in front of you. Start with a handful of strikes and the assembled payoff is a jagged approximation with visible corners; add strikes and the corners round off onto the smooth log curve. In numbers, on a chain running from 40% to 250% of the forward against a true 25% volatility: strikes every $40 recover 22.35% , every $10 recover 25.02% , and every $2.50 recover 25.00% . Twenty-one strikes is already enough to be within two basis points. That convergence is fast and it is the reassuring half of the story. The alarming half is the next chapter, because none of those numbers survive if you shorten the range rather than the spacing. [equation: strip weight at strike K ∝ ΔK / K²] Reads as: buy more of the low strikes and less of the high ones, in proportion to one over the strike squared. A $50 option gets sixteen times the weight of a $200 one. The strip's payoff converging onto the log contract Recovered volatility against strike spacing The chain Watch the corners rather than the overall shape — the strip is already roughly right with six strikes, and what the extra strikes buy is the removal of kinks between them. Each kink is a place where your replication is a straight line and the true payoff is curved, which is exactly where a variance measurement goes missing. Try this Take the spacing out to $40 and count the corners. Predict whether a coarse strip over-measures or under-measures variance before you read the number.

chapters.title: The wings are not a detail either
chapters.dek: Cut the strike range to 92%–108% and a 25 variance swap prices at 17.4. The strikes nobody wants to quote are a third of the contract.

figures.title: Where a variance swap's value actually comes from
figures.caption: Drag the lower bound alone and watch the recovered volatility fall much faster than dragging the upper bound by the same amount. The asymmetry is the 1/K² weight: truncating the downside removes heavily weighted options, truncating the upside removes lightly weighted ones. A variance swap is, structurally, mostly a position in the put wing.

checks.q: A market maker quotes you a variance swap on a name whose listed options stop at 85% and 120% of spot. What have they actually sold you?
checks.right: A truncated approximation plus their own view on the unlisted wings, worth about 17% of the contract at that range. The wing risk did not disappear; it moved onto their book
checks.why: An approximation plus somebody's wing mark. The contract is perfectly writable and it is exactly as hedgeable as the strikes available to hedge it. Whatever the strip cannot reach is warehoused risk, priced from a model rather than a market — which is why variance swaps on illiquid underlyings are quoted wide and why they behave badly in exactly the moves that were supposed to make them pay.

chapters.text: Chapter 03 showed the strip converging quickly in the number of strikes. It is easy to read that as "the replication is robust" and it is the wrong lesson, because the quantity that matters is not how finely the strikes are spaced but how far they extend. Hold the spacing at $5 and pull the range in. From 40%–250% of the forward the strip recovers 24.97% against a true 25%. Narrow it to 75%–140% and you get 23.69% . Narrow again to 85%–120% — still a wider range than many single-name chains actually quote — and you get 20.81% , low by 16.8% . At 92%–108% the answer is 17.42% , low by 30.3% , on a contract that was supposed to be replicable. The reason is the 1/K² weight, which is doing something people consistently underestimate. Low strikes get enormous weight — a 50 strike carries sixteen times the weight of a 200 strike — and while each of those options is individually cheap, there are a lot of them and the weighting is aggressive. Break the total down by where it comes from and the at-the-money region between 90% and 110% supplies only 50.7% of the variance. The band from 70% to 90% supplies 22.9% , and everything below 70% another 3.5% . So roughly a quarter of a variance swap's value lives in strikes below 90%, in options that are individually near-worthless, frequently untradeable in size, and quoted on a volatility that is largely a market-maker's opinion. That is the practical fragility of the product, and it is why the honest version of "variance is replicable" carries the words "given a continuum of strikes" in front of it. Where a variance swap's value actually comes from Recovered volatility as the range is truncated The listed range Drag the lower bound alone and watch the recovered volatility fall much faster than dragging the upper bound by the same amount. The asymmetry is the 1/K² weight: truncating the downside removes heavily weighted options, truncating the upside removes lightly weighted ones. A variance swap is, structurally, mostly a position in the put wing. [equation: σ_R² ≈ (2e^rT/T) · Σ (ΔK/K²) · O(K)] Reads as: add up every out-of-the-money option, each weighted by one over its strike squared. O(K) means the put below the forward and the call above it — always the out-of-the-money side, because that is the one that trades. Try this Set the range to 85%–120%, which is a plausible listed chain on a mid-cap. Predict the recovered volatility, then read it. Then move only the lower bound to 60%.

chapters.title: What the contract actually pays
chapters.dek: Quoted in volatility points, settled in variance, and convex in a direction that matters enormously to whoever is short.

figures.title: Payoff against realized volatility, and a linear vega position for comparison
figures.caption: The gap between the curve and the straight line is the convexity, and it is the reason the product exists. Long variance, it is a gift: you are paid more per point the further you are right. Short variance, it is the whole risk, and it arrives precisely in the scenario — a violent move — where you are least able to do anything about it.

checks.q: The at-the-money vol is 25 and the variance strike is 30.4. What is the market saying?
checks.right: Almost nothing about the expected level. The 5.4-point gap is the skew being mechanically averaged in by the 1/K² weights — the put wing is expensive, and a variance strike is an average over the whole surface
checks.why: It is a statement about the surface's shape, not its level. This is the single most common misreading of a variance quote, and it has a real consequence: comparing a variance strike to an at-the-money volatility and calling the difference "the variance risk premium" double-counts the skew. Strip the skew contribution out first, or you are measuring the smile and calling it a forecast.

chapters.text: A variance swap is quoted as a volatility — "we'll trade var at 25" — and settles on variance. The payoff is the difference of the squares, scaled by a notional, and that mismatch between the quoting convention and the settlement convention is where most of the practical confusion lives. Because nobody wants to think in units of variance, the market sizes these in vega notional : the amount you make or lose for the first volatility point of difference. Variance notional is then vega notional divided by twice the strike. The consequence is that the first point behaves like a normal vega position and every subsequent point pays more than the one before. Run the numbers on a 25 strike with $100,000 of vega notional. Realized comes in at 26 and you make about $100,000. At 30, a five-point miss, you make roughly $550,000 — not five times the one-point figure but five and a half. At 45 you make $2.8 million . On the other side, realized at 20 loses you about $450,000 and realized at 10 loses $1.05 million , which is where the asymmetry shows: volatility cannot go below zero, so the short's losses are unbounded while the long's are capped at the strike. One more thing the strip explains rather than assumes. The fair variance strike is not the at-the-money volatility — it is an average over the whole surface with 1/K² weights, so skew pushes it up . On a 25% at-the-money vol, a skew of −0.10 gives a variance strike of 25.75% , and a skew of −0.25 gives 30.40% . That five-and-a-half-point premium is not a forecast that the stock will be more volatile. It is the put wing being expensive, mechanically loaded into a single number. [equation: payoff = N_vega · (σ_R² − K_var²) / (2·K_var)] Reads as: you are paid the difference of the squares, sized so that the first volatility point is worth your vega notional. The division by twice the strike is purely the unit conversion that makes the quote readable. Long variance, it is a gift: you are paid more per point the further you are right. Short variance, it is the whole risk, and it arrives precisely in the scenario — a violent move — where you are least able to do anything about it. chapters.title: VIX is this, implemented
chapters.dek: Not a forecast, not a sentiment gauge. A 30-day variance strip with a published rulebook.

figures.title: The 30-day strip, and the index it produces
figures.caption: The bars are what the index is actually made of. Notice how much of the total sits to the left of the forward even though those options are the cheap ones — that is the 1/K² weight, and it is why the index responds so strongly to the put wing being bid.

checks.q: Thirty-day at-the-money implied volatility is unchanged on the day, but the index is up two points. What is the most likely explanation?
checks.right: Skew steepened, or bids appeared in deeper puts and extended the strip. Both raise a 1/K²-weighted average without moving the at-the-money option
checks.why: The wing repriced. The index is a weighted average across the whole surface, so it can move a long way with the at-the-money option untouched — and on a lot of days that is exactly what happens. Reading the index as a level of fear rather than as an average of a shape is the most common mistake made about it.

chapters.text: The index everyone quotes as "the fear gauge" is the calculation from chapter 03 run on a fixed schedule. It takes out-of-the-money options on two expiries bracketing 30 days, weights each by ΔK/K² , adds them up, interpolates between the two expiries to land exactly on 30 days, and reports the square root as an annualized percentage. There is no model in it, no volatility forecast, and no opinion. Three consequences follow directly from the chapters above, and each explains something people find puzzling about the index. First, it is a variance strike, so it carries the skew premium. VIX sits above at-the-money 30-day implied volatility essentially always, and the gap widens when skew steepens. That is chapter 05's 5.4 points, not the market becoming more afraid. Second, it inherits the truncation problem. The rulebook stops including strikes once it meets two consecutive zero bids, so the effective wing of the strip is set by what happens to be quoted that morning. In a stressed market more deep puts get bids, the strip extends, and the index rises partly because more of the tail became visible. Third, it is a strike, not an asset. You cannot hold VIX. What trades is a futures contract on where the index will be, which is a different thing with its own term structure and its own roll — and that is the source of the long-run behavior of every product built on top of it. The figure runs the calculation on a synthetic chain so you can watch the index move for structural reasons rather than emotional ones: steepen the skew and it rises with volatility unchanged; truncate the quoted wing and it falls with everything else held fixed. The 30-day strip, and the index it produces This morning's chain The bars are what the index is actually made of. Notice how much of the total sits to the left of the forward even though those options are the cheap ones — that is the 1/K² weight, and it is why the index responds so strongly to the put wing being bid.

chapters.title: Where it breaks
chapters.dek: The replication is exact under one assumption that markets violate on their most important days.

figures.title: What the strip prices against what actually happens, with jumps
figures.caption: The two curves separate as the jump gets larger and more negative, and they separate in the direction that hurts a hedger. Notice also that upward jumps of the same size do not produce the same gap — the logarithm is asymmetric, which is the same asymmetry that makes the put wing dominate chapter 04.

checks.q: You are long variance through the replicating strip — long the options, delta-hedged — rather than through a swap. The stock gaps down 25% overnight on a takeover collapse. What happens?
checks.right: You make money, but less than the realized variance suggests. The strip prices the log contract, and under a jump that is not quite quadratic variation — the gap runs to about a point of volatility
checks.why: You make money, and you under-collect. Being long variance through a crash is the right side of the trade and the replication still leaves a gap, because the argument that made it exact assumed the price never skipped. This is the honest reason variance swaps on single names carry caps and wide bid–offers: the product's one structural weakness shows up in the one scenario that defines it.

chapters.text: Chapter 02's derivation used Itô's lemma, and Itô's lemma assumes the price path is continuous. A jump moves the stock a finite distance in no time, with no opportunity to rebalance in between, and the neat cancellation that made the log contract a variance meter does not survive it. The consequence is a bias with a definite sign. The log contract prices −(2/T)·E[ln(S_T/F)] , and under jumps that quantity is no longer the expected quadratic variation. On a 20% diffusive volatility with one expected jump a year of −20% , true quadratic variation corresponds to 29.97% while the strip prices 29.38% — the replication is 0.59 volatility points light . With a −30% jump expected once every two years the gap widens to 1.10 points ; twice a year, to 2.62 . The strip under-hedges a downward-jumping stock, and it does so exactly when the contract is paying out most. Three more failures worth naming, none of them exotic. Discreteness. The contract settles on daily closing returns, not on a continuous integral. That introduces sampling error with no bias, which the chapter 02 figure shows directly when you drop the hedge count. Caps. Most single-name variance swaps are sold with a cap, usually at two and a half times the strike. That cap makes the payoff no longer variance — it is a variance swap minus a call on variance — and the replication chapter no longer applies to the capped part. The cap exists because of everything above. Liquidity in the wing. Chapter 04's arithmetic assumed you could buy every strike at the quoted price. In the move that makes a variance swap pay, the put wing gaps and widens simultaneously, so the hedge you needed becomes expensive precisely when you need to put it on. None of this makes the product unsound. It makes the phrase "variance is perfectly replicable" a statement about a model rather than about a market, and the gap between those two is the entire job. What the strip prices against what actually happens, with jumps The jump The two curves separate as the jump gets larger and more negative, and they separate in the direction that hurts a hedger. Notice also that upward jumps of the same size do not produce the same gap — the logarithm is asymmetric, which is the same asymmetry that makes the put wing dominate chapter 04.

chapters.title: Marking it before expiry
chapters.dek: Halfway through its life a variance swap is two things: realized variance already banked, and a new swap on the variance still to come.

figures.title: Mark-to-market against the implied vol for the rest of the life
figures.caption: The upper curve is a parabola, because the new swap is on variance. The lower curve climbs ever more steeply as the time left shrinks: a shortfall in realized variance gets harder to make up the less time remains to make it up in.

figures.title: Short variance through a crash
figures.caption: For 29 quiet days realized vol runs at 13.5 and the short swap is up $250,000, a little less than the vol swap's $268,000. Then the stock gaps 9%. The variance swap is marked at a loss of $1.61 million the same evening, against $1.23 million for the vol swap, reaches $1.81 million on day 40, and expires down $1.41 million with realized at 31.0; the vol swap ends down $1.10 million. Short variance earns less when it is quiet and loses more when it is not. That is what the square does.

checks.q: Long a one-year variance swap struck at 25, three quarters through its life, realized so far 25, implied for the rest 25. What is it worth?
checks.why: Zero. Banked and forward variance both equal the strike's, so the bracket is zero. A variance swap has no time decay of its own; it only has the gap between what has happened, what is now expected, and what was agreed.

chapters.text: You are long a one-year variance swap struck at 25, with $100,000 of vega notional. Six months have passed and the stock has realized 20. The figure marks the position against the implied volatility for the remaining six months, which is what you would have to strike a new swap at today. Mark-to-market against the implied vol for the rest of the life Implied vol the rest of the life must reach to break even The swap so far The upper curve is a parabola, because the new swap is on variance. The lower curve climbs ever more steeply as the time left shrinks: a shortfall in realized variance gets harder to make up the less time remains to make it up in. [equation: MTM = N_var × [ (t/T)·σ_realized² + (1 − t/T)·K_now² − K² ] × DF N_var = N_vega / (2K)] Reads as: the variance banked so far, weighted by the time it covered, plus the variance a new swap would lock in for the time left, minus the strike's variance, all times the variance notional and discounted to the payment date. Every volatility here is in points, as in chapter 05. The variance notional is $100,000 divided by twice 25: $2,000 per point squared. Half a year at 20 banks 200; half a year at an implied 25 adds 312.5; together 512.5 against the strike's 625. The shortfall of 112.5 points squared is worth −$225,000 , or −$220,545 discounted for six months at 4%. The implied vol going forward is exactly the strike, and the position is still deeply under water, because half the variance it was promised did not happen. To get back to zero the remaining six months have to be struck at 29.15 . With three months left that number is 36.06; with five weeks left it is 51.48. And the position's vega shrinks as the life runs out: halfway through, a point on the remaining implied vol is worth about $50,000 , half the notional, because only half the life is still exposed to it. This is how a desk marks the book every night, and it explains two things traders say about variance swaps. A long position that has under-realized is "dead": it needs an implausible vol for the rest of the life. And because realized variance is banked as it happens, a variance swap carries its daily P&L in the realized term even when implied vol does not move, which an option book of the same vega does not. Try this Let the stock realize 30 for the first half instead. Predict the mark if implied for the rest is still 25. Now hold one through a bad quarter. You sold a 63-day variance swap at 20 vol on $100,000 of vega notional, which makes every variance point worth $2,500. Step through the days: each one moves realized variance and the market's implied vol for what is left, and the swap is marked on both. Somewhere in here the stock gaps. You can buy the swap back at the mark whenever you like. A vol swap of the same size runs alongside for comparison. Short variance through a crash Your swap For 29 quiet days realized vol runs at 13.5 and the short swap is up $250,000, a little less than the vol swap's $268,000. Then the stock gaps 9%. The variance swap is marked at a loss of $1.61 million the same evening, against $1.23 million for the vol swap, reaches $1.81 million on day 40, and expires down $1.41 million with realized at 31.0; the vol swap ends down $1.10 million. Short variance earns less when it is quiet and loses more when it is not. That is what the square does. Trader's lens Selling variance is selling insurance with an uncapped payout: the premium is the gap between implied and the realized vol of quiet markets, and the claims arrive in the few days that are not quiet. Desks that sell it watch the convexity, the extra loss variance carries over vol in a large move, more than the carry, and buy it back or cap it before the gap rather than after. One gap day can carry a whole quarter's realized variance. Variance is dominated by its largest observations. The mark moves twice in a crash: realized jumps, and implied for the remaining days jumps with it. Capped variance swaps exist because the dealers on the other side know exactly this. Rule of thumb: a short variance swap's loss in a move is about vega notional × (realized² − strike²) ÷ (2 × strike), and it grows with the square.

chapters.title: Check yourself
chapters.dek: Six questions across the page. Each explanation names the chapter to revisit.

checks.q: When are a variance swap and a volatility swap worth the same?
checks.right: Only when realized volatility is known in advance. Any uncertainty about it opens a convexity gap — 2.08 volatility points at a vol of vol of 0.4
checks.why: Only under certainty. A flat surface removes the skew premium of chapter 05 but does nothing to Jensen — the gap here is about uncertainty in the outcome, not about the shape of today's smile.

checks.q: What makes the log contract special?
checks.right: Its dollar gamma is constant, so a delta hedge earns the same for a percentage move at any price level — which is what makes the accumulated P&L equal realized variance
checks.why: Constant dollar gamma. Ordinary options have a dollar-gamma hill centered on their strike, so they measure movement only where they are standing. The logarithm is the one payoff whose second derivative cancels the S² and leaves a flat meter.

checks.q: Where does the 1/K² weighting come from?
checks.right: From the second derivative of the log payoff. Any payoff decomposes into options weighted by its own curvature, and for −ln(S) that curvature is 1/S²
checks.why: It is the curvature of a logarithm. The static replication result says a twice-differentiable payoff equals a fixed portfolio of options weighted by its second derivative at each strike. Everything else about the weight is a consequence.

checks.q: Which change damages the replication more: doubling the strike spacing, or halving the strike range?
checks.right: Halving the range, by a wide margin. Going from $5 to $10 spacing costs about 6 basis points; pulling the range from 40–250% to 92–108% costs 758 basis points
checks.why: The range, and it is not close. Convergence in spacing is fast and convergence in range is slow, which is the opposite of most people's intuition and the reason variance products are fragile on names with thin wings.

checks.q: Realized volatility comes in at 10 against a 25 strike. You were short $100,000 of vega notional. Roughly what did you make?
checks.right: About $1.05 million. Convexity works against the short in both directions: fifteen points down pays less than the linear $1.5 million, and fifteen points up would have cost $1.95 million
checks.why: About $1.05 million. The payoff is in the difference of squares, so the same number of points is worth less further below the strike and more further above it. That asymmetry is the entire risk profile: bounded gains, unbounded losses.

checks.q: Why do single-name variance swaps usually carry a cap?
checks.right: Because the replication fails exactly where the payoff is largest — jumps break the log-contract argument and the wing becomes untradeable in a crash, so the short is selling a risk they cannot hedge
checks.why: Because the tail is the unhedgeable part. A cap converts the contract into a variance swap minus a call on variance, which is an admission that the replication argument stops working in the scenario the contract is really about.
